content:
HONG KONG — A year after the fire that took his wife's life, Yip Ka Kui still sends her voice messages and photos on WhatsApp, as if she had only gone away on a trip.

His wife, Pak Sui Lin, was among the 168 people killed when fire tore through the Wang Fuk Court housing estate in Hong Kong's Tai Po district on November 26 last year — the deadliest blaze in the city since 1948. On Thursday, exactly one year on, former residents were expected to return to the estate to mark the anniversary of a disaster that destroyed their homes and, for many, their sense of safety.

The fire ripped through seven of the estate's eight 31-storey residential blocks, where renovation work was under way and the buildings were wrapped in bamboo scaffolding and dust netting. It burned for more than 43 hours, displaced nearly 5,000 residents and left the towers blackened and empty behind police patrols and fences. The towers remain vacant today, their scorched facades still visible from the street.

For the survivors, the past twelve months have been, in their own words, survival mode. Many spent the year attending hearings held by a judge-led panel investigating the disaster, following debates over long-term housing, and mourning in public as well as in private. Phyllis Lo, 49, who lost her mother in the fire, told Reuters she had put much of her own work aside to follow the inquiry. "I lost part of my youth," she said. "In the past year I spent so much time following the hearings and watching the news."

The inquiry, whose findings were published last month, gave the families something they had waited almost a year to hear: a detailed account of how the fire started, how it spread so fast, and who was to blame. According to the independent committee's report, the blaze was most likely ignited by a lit cigarette on a flat roof between two first-floor apartments in Wang Cheong House, where construction workers had been smoking. But the cigarette was only the spark. What turned a small fire into a catastrophe was everything around it.

The committee found that fire-retardant scaffolding nets had been substituted with non-fire-retardant ones, that windows were covered with non-fire-retardant foam boards, and that openings had been cut into the escape staircases for workers' convenience. Most of the victims died not from burns but from smoke inhalation: the altered staircases let smoke flood the escape routes, the foam boards blocked residents' views and delayed evacuation, and the estate's fire alarm system had been shut down. The report named the renovation contractor, Prestige Construction & Engineering, and the project consultant, Will Power Architects, as the main culprits, saying there was "no doubt" they bore responsibility for the inferno and the high death toll. It also found that four government departments — the Housing Bureau's independent checking unit, the Buildings Department, the Fire Services Department and the Labour Department — had failed in their supervisory duties.

The political fallout came swiftly. Hong Kong leader John Lee apologised on behalf of the government — the first such gesture since the fire — and announced the resignation of Housing Secretary Winnie Ho, the first official to step down over the disaster. He promised sweeping reforms to the building industry and the regulatory system, including laws to criminalise bid rigging in the lucrative renovation sector. The committee made 120 recommendations in all, including bans on combustible foam boards on windows and external walls, a ban on new openings in escape stairs, and phased external works on large multi-block projects so that not every tower is wrapped in scaffolding at once.

For many families, however, the reforms have done little to ease the feeling of injustice. "Why is it that mistakes made by certain individuals and the inaction of some government departments led to such a major disaster, yet it is us, the victims, who are left to pay the price?" Yip asked, according to [Reuters](https://www.straitstimes.com/asia/one-year-after-hong-kong-fire-survivors-mourn-losses-and-question-accountability).

The practical question of where the displaced residents will live remains unresolved for many. The government has offered homeowners a buyback scheme and access to replacement subsidised flats, and most owners have accepted the plan, which officials describe as the fastest way to help residents rebuild their lives. But the government has ruled out rebuilding the estate on its original site, citing the lengthy process involved — a decision that has left some residents feeling they have lost not just a home but a root. "I lost a root. This is my family home. I have lived here for 40 years; it was a place I could fall back on when something happened," Lo said.

The anniversary itself has become a test of how the city is allowed to remember. Hong Kong's Chief Secretary, Eric Chan, said this week that while the government would not organise any memorial events, it would not prevent citizens from taking part in legal commemorative activities. The Catholic diocese has asked parishes across the city to hold special masses for the victims on the anniversary. Some residents hope the government will build a permanent monument listing the names of all 168 victims on the original site, which is planned to become a park.

Shortly after the fire, Beijing warned it would crack down on any "anti-China" protest, and the authorities shut down an online petition demanding an independent probe, as public anger grew over missed fire-risk warnings and evidence of unsafe construction practices. The independent inquiry eventually happened anyway, and its report — more than 1,000 pages, drawn from 30 days of hearings between March and July — is now public, except for some 41 pages redacted to avoid prejudicing ongoing criminal proceedings.

The lessons of Wang Fuk Court reach beyond Hong Kong. The same combination of flammable temporary materials, weakened escape routes and lax supervision exists in renovation projects across Asia's dense cities, and the inquiry's findings have become a case study in what can go wrong when cost-cutting meets weak oversight. Hong Kong's own regulators are now under a three-month investigation to determine whether staff were derelict in their duties — a process the families are watching closely.

A year on, the estate that was home to around 2,000 families stands empty. The residents who return on Thursday will find the towers still fenced off, the blackened concrete still there, and the questions that have followed them for a year still unanswered: who will be held criminally responsible, and whether the reforms promised in October will actually prevent the next Wang Fuk Court. For Yip, the answer is simpler and more personal. Six months ago he returned to the charred flat he had shared with his wife for more than two decades, stood in the dark apartment and called out into the silence: "Don't stay here. Go wherever you want to; you're free now." Then he went home and kept texting her, every day.

Hong Kong remains one of Asia's most closely watched financial centres, and the disaster has also raised questions about the city's governance that extend well beyond housing policy — as seen in [recent developments in the city](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/china-2-billion-dollar-sovereign-bonds-hong-kong-november-2026). For the families of Wang Fuk Court, though, the anniversary is not about policy. It is about 168 people who did not come home — including a firefighter who died in the line of duty — and about a year of grief that, as one resident put it, has not passed a single day without thinking of that afternoon.
summary: A year after the Wang Fuk Court blaze killed 168 people, survivors and bereaved families returned to the charred Tai Po estate on Thursday to mark the anniversary — grieving, still displaced, and still asking why warnings were ignored.
title: One year after Hong Kong's deadliest fire in decades, survivors return to Tai Po still waiting for justice
